6. System Overview
The Quantitative Systems platform comprises services and pipelines that deliver analytics and curated data to front-office, risk, and finance consumers. Core components include QS-Core (APP-QS-001), an API-driven analytics layer for pricing, sensitivities, and scenario outputs; QS-Stream (APP-QS-002), an ingestion and transformation framework for market and reference data; QS-Calc (APP-QS-003), a batch/grid computation orchestrator supporting end-of-day and intraday cycles; QS-UI (APP-QS-004), presentation tools for scenario configuration and monitoring; and the Model Catalog Connector (APP-QS-006), which synchronizes registration metadata and lifecycle states with MRM repositories. Environments are segregated by lifecycle (Development, Integration, UAT, Production) with standard promotion controls and artifact tagging. Business criticality ratings per BIA-QS-2026-RevC classify QS-Core and QS-Calc as Tier 1 services, QS-Stream as Tier 2, and QS-UI/Connector as Tier 3. Data classification within QS-Stream includes Firm Confidential and Public categories as defined in the Enterprise Data Classification Standard (EDO-CLASS-2024). No sensitive personal data resides in the platform per the Privacy Impact Assessment PIA-QS-2025-01, reaffirmed 2026-02-27.

Integration points with the Risk Data Warehouse (RDW) and Regulatory Reporting Extracts (RRE) follow standardized publish/subscribe patterns with documented schemas and release communications. Operational responsibilities are split between QE (development, release, configuration of models and analytics) and PRE (runtime operations, monitoring, incident coordination). EDO provides stewardship for CDEs flowing through QS-Stream, ensuring data quality rules are cataloged and aligned to enterprise standards. Model Risk Management maintains independence and oversight for model validation and governs the Model Catalog, with defined checkpoints for code artifact identification and deployment readiness.

7. Control Environment Summary
Change and release management processes for QS follow TRC-SDLC-001 and TRC-SM-003. Standard changes require peer review, automated testing evidence, impact assessments, and approval from designated change approvers; emergency changes require post-implementation review within two business days. Observed adherence in sampled changes included traceable links from change requests to deployment tags and regression testing artifacts. Release communications were disseminated through the established channel (DL-QS-Release-Notice) at least 24 hours prior to production implementation, with closures documented in ServiceNow. Access governance aligns to TRC-AG-002 with role-based access mapped to defined entitlements; quarterly recertification was completed for Q2 FY2026 (AG-RC-2026-QS, attested by QE and PRE managers). Service management incorporates incident and problem workflows with SLA tracking, service health dashboards, and retrospective reviews for Sev2 events.

Data governance is anchored by EDO-DG-001 and includes stewardship assignments, lineage documentation, and data quality monitoring. For QS-Stream, rule definitions and thresholds are documented in the Data Quality Catalog (DQ-CAT-QS-Stream, version 2026.05). Operational resilience for Tier 1 services includes documented recovery objectives, runbooks, and scenario testing per TRC-BCP-005. Third-party assurance for critical services is tracked under Vendor Risk Management (VRM) with the latest SOC reports reviewed and mapped to control coverage matrices (VRM-ASSUR-2026-QS).

Build artifacts were appropriately referenced (Jenkins job QS-CI-Release build #982, completed 2026-02-18 01:12 UTC), and pre-implementation testing evidence was present for 29/30 sampled changes (96.7%). The exception (CHG0011607) lacked an attached functional test summary at approval time; the artifact was subsequently uploaded (2026-02-19 10:22 EST) with eCAB notation and no adverse outcomes.

Execution quality and post-implementation review. Change failure rate for the quarter was 0.6% (1 of 184), with a single change rolled back due to a validation query error in a non-critical reporting job (CHG0011554; associated incident INC0019520 opened 2026-03-05 00:37 UTC; resolved 03:41 UTC). Emergency changes (n=3: CHG0011734, CHG0011798, CHG0011831) were appropriately invoked in response to vendor-side anomalies and executed under expedited approvals, followed by mandatory retrospectives documented by Production Assurance (PA-SO-2026-0252, -0261, -0267). All three retrospectives identified clear preventive actions, which were tracked to closure in JIRA (QSYS-2231, QSYS-2237, DE-MP-1479).

Control evidence and linkage to operational stability. Post-implementation monitoring evidence (30–60 minute observation logs with sign-offs) was present in 100% of sampled standard/normal changes. Where incidents occurred within 24 hours of change (n=4; INC0019459, INC0019481, INC0019520, INC0019568), mean time to resolve was 3.2 hours, and root cause attribution was completed within two business days in each case. None of the incidents led to missed reporting deadlines or incomplete risk runs, and two were traced to external dependencies (vendor feed delays) rather than release defects. The change calendar reflected appropriate blackout observance around month-end risk cycles.

Process maturity and data quality of the change register. The change register was complete and timely, with accurate linkages to impacted configuration items and downstream applications. Minor inconsistencies were noted in the naming convention of deployment packages across QSYS-Core and Data Ingestion (e.g., QS-PLAT-2026.3.14 vs. QS-PLATFORM-2026_03_14), which can hinder automated reporting. Management has initiated a standardization exercise (QSYS-OPS-STD-2026-05) with a target effective date of 2026-06-30. Additionally, the free-text “success/failure rationale” field was sparsely populated in 5 of 30 sampled records; while evidence existed elsewhere, completing this field would strengthen auditability.

Conclusion and rating. Change management controls are effective. Approvals are timely, segregation of duties is maintained, and execution quality is high with a low failure rate. Minor enhancements to artifact attachment discipline and naming standardization are underway and, in our assessment, do not materially impact control effectiveness. Management has accepted the observations with remediation dates aligned to Q3 FY2026 and designated accountable owners within QS Ops and DE-MP.
Section 6: Data Governance and Lineage Controls

6.1 Overview and Scope
For FY2026, the Internal Audit function evaluated Meridian Capital’s data governance implementation supporting Quantitative Systems (QSYS) with a focus on market, reference, and derived datasets that serve pricing models, intraday risk analytics, and end-of-day valuations. The assessment encompassed lineage registration, data quality controls, exception management workflows, and archival/retention conformance. Evidence was obtained via repository extracts from the enterprise data catalog (Atlas v3.9), control attestations filed by Data Governance Office (DGO) and Quant Platform Engineering (QPE), and targeted sampling of data pipelines supporting datasets DS-MKTD-0012 (equities consolidated tape), DS-FXSP-0041 (spot FX intraday), and DS-REFD-0090 (security master reference clusters), with corroboration against ServiceNow and Jira tickets logged between 2025-10-01 and 2026-05-31.

6.2 Data Sourcing and Lineage Registration
Primary and contingent sourcing paths for each in-scope dataset are registered in the enterprise catalog with upstream provider identifiers, normalization stages, and consumer mappings to model families QMOD-EQ-PRC-Alpha and QMOD-FX-Vol-SV. Lineage coverage across the QSYS domain improved from 91% (FY2025) to 96% (FY2026 YTD) based on control DGO-LNG-004 scorecards (report DGO-Score-2026Q2, 2026-05-27 13:14Z). The residual 4% pertains to intraday OTC quote enrichments aggregated by Market Data Operations (MDO) for select fixed income instruments where limited metadata is passed through ad hoc staging. This gap is documented (ticket DGO-1637, opened 2026-03-06 10:22Z) with remediation in progress to harmonize enrichment steps and register full upstream identifiers; target status is “On Track” with a forecast close of 2026-08-31 pending UAT by QPE.

Lineage paths include explicit stage identifiers (STG-QSYS-ING, NRM-QSYS-STD, CRT-QSYS-DER) and completion timestamps. Audit sampling validated that consumer mappings reflect actual dependencies observed in Airflow run histories for 28 out of 30 sampled jobs; two mappings (Airflow DAG IDs qsys_fx_spot_norm_v2, qsys_eq_adjclose_roll_v4) still reference deprecated consumers in non-production only; a cleanup task (QSYS-28401) has been filed with no downstream risk declared.

6.3 Data Quality Controls and Exception Handling
Quality checks across ingestion and normalization include field-level null thresholds, schema compatibility checks, and cross-provider reconciliation counts implemented under control set QPE-QC-07 to QPE-QC-14. For DS-FXSP-0041, reconciliations against provider day-close totals (QC-11) showed 99.8% pass rate over the period, with four amber events in February 2026 relating to provider maintenance windows (ServiceNow INC0019453 opened 2026-02-14 07:28Z; resolved 2026-02-14 10:16Z; MTTR 2h48m). Exception handling follows documented runbook references in the Quality Incident Register (QIR) with automated ticket creation for red threshold breaches and batch rechecks at T+15 minutes for transient vendor gaps. No critical red breaches were recorded for QSYS during Q2 FY2026.

Schema drift detection (QC-12) flagged one change on 2026-02-05 07:12Z for a new optional field introduced by the alternate market data provider within equities corporate action feeds. The alert was triaged within 12 minutes by MDO (ticket MDO-CA-7713) and normalized in the staging layer following standard governance review (Change CHG0017761 approved 2026-02-05 08:03Z, CAB reference CAB-2026-W05-QSYS). No consumer impact was observed; downstream models treated the new attribute as non-material pending prioritization by the Quant Research Council (QRC).

For DS-REFD-0090, attribute completeness checkpoints (QC-09) over security master clusters achieved a 99.2% completeness score, down modestly from 99.4% in FY2025, primarily due to delayed LEI refreshes for newly listed small-cap issuers (MDO backlog report MDO-REF-Rep-2026Q2). The Data Governance Office flagged the trend as within tolerance but recommended continued weekly monitoring; QPE’s response plan and tracking (QSYS-28917) indicate corrective actions are underway with MDO to align refresh cadence with listing surges during earnings seasons.

6.4 Data Timeliness and SLAs
Timeliness adherence for ingestion and normalization phases against published SLAs (POL-DATA-SLA-06) was measured across 1,482 batch instances. SLA attainment averaged 99.3% across trading days, with nine instances of minor lateness (<7 minutes) during daylight saving transitions in March 2026. These were pre-communicated by Enterprise Scheduling Services (ESS) (Advisory ESS-ADV-2026-03-07) and tracked as known events. No downstream model recalculation windows were breached; capacity buffers absorbed the delays, and operational metrics remained green in the QSYS Command Center dashboard for the relevant days.

6.5 Retention, Archival, and Disposal
Retention and archival practices for raw ticks, normalized snapshots, and derived aggregates were reviewed against policy POL-DATA-RET-09 and procedure DGO-PRO-RET-04. Raw ticks for DS-MKTD-0012 are retained for 13 months in warm storage with quarterly certified archives to compliant cold storage tiers; normalized snapshots are held for 36 months; derived aggregates for 60 months. Compliance for Q1–Q3 FY2026 was 100% based on storage certification attestations (STOR-ATT-2026Q3). In Q4 FY2026 to date, one variance was recorded: the March 2026 quarterly archive for DS-FXSP-0041 completed with a 48-hour delay due to a capacity rebalancing event within the cold tier (ticket STOR-2298 opened 2026-04-02 02:11Z, closed 2026-04-04 04:29Z). No data loss or integrity issues were identified; the event remained within the grace period contemplated by the policy and was communicated via standard variance reporting to DGO.

6.6 Quality Scorecards and Governance Reporting
Monthly data quality scorecards (DGO-SC-2026-01 to -05) show consistent performance within thresholds: weighted composite scores of 4.5/5 for FX spot and 4.1/5 for equities consolidated tape, versus a minimum acceptable composite of 4.0/5 per QSYS standards. Trend analysis highlights stable reconciliation rates and improved null-handling in security master clusters following attribute normalization deployed in January 2026 (Change CHG0017029, implemented 2026-01-19 21:47Z). Governance reporting to the Model Oversight and Review Committee (MORC) includes a quarterly lineage coverage update and a listing of open data-related corrective actions. As of 2026-05-31, three corrective actions remain open for the QSYS domain (DGO-1637; QSYS-28917; MDO-CA-7713), all categorized as low to moderate operational impact with established target closure timelines and identified accountable owners.



Section 7: Change Management, Model Governance, and Operational Monitoring

7.1 Change Management and Release Governance
Internal Audit reviewed QSYS change and release practices across application code, model parameter sets, and data transformation logic for the period 2025-10-01 to 2026-05-31. Evidence was drawn from ServiceNow Change records (CHG0016684–CHG0018129), Jira epics and stories (e.g., QSYS-Rel-Q2.3.17; QSYS-28401; QSYS-29103), and CAB minutes (CAB-2026-W07-QSYS through CAB-2026-W21-QSYS). The release cadence remained biweekly for non-critical updates, with documented freeze windows around quarter-ends. Segregation of duties was consistently observed: 100% of sampled production changes (n=42) had peer code review recorded by a team member not involved in the originating development (reviewers from QPE-Pricing Core and QPE-Data Services), and 100% had explicit approvals from Change Owners and CAB delegates.

Approval timeliness across standard changes met internal targets in 92% of cases; three changes experienced approval lag exceeding four hours due to multi-region sign-off coordination (CHG0017792, CHG0017831, CHG0018045). These were pre-classified as low-risk parameter refreshes and executed within the same business day. Two emergency changes were logged during the period (CHG-E001122, 2026-03-18 12:34Z; CHG-E001137, 2026-04-26 06:51Z) to accommodate a non-disruptive vendor field label update and a minor compatibility patch within a normalization routine. Both were pre-authorized under established emergency criteria and followed with post-implementation reviews (PIR) within 48 hours.

Automated validation coverage improved: unit test coverage for core pricing libraries increased from 78% to 84% per Q1–Q2 trend reports (QPE-QA-Rep-2026Q2). Pipeline regression checks for data transforms recorded a 99.2% pass rate, with transient failures linked to provider-side test endpoints during off-market hours. No deviations from documented deployment steps were observed in the sample, and rollback verification entries were present for all sampled changes.

7.2 Model Governance and Oversight
Model lifecycle controls for the QSYS domain align with Meridian Capital’s Model Risk Management Standard (MRM-STD-2024-R2). Audit testing covered model registration, validation attestations, periodic performance reviews, and ongoing monitoring operated by the Quant Risk Analytics (QRA) team. During the period, one new model version, QMOD-FX-Vol-SV v4.5, entered controlled production on 2026-04-12 21:47Z following MORC endorsement (MORC-Min-2026-04-08). Validation artifacts (QRA-VAL-2026-014) included challenger–champion analyses, sensitivity testing summaries, and implementation verification signed by QPE. All required sign-offs were obtained, including Data Governance confirmation on input suitability (DGO-CFM-2026-031) and Legal/Compliance acknowledgment of use case alignment.

Backtesting results for QMOD-EQ-PRC-Alpha over the trailing six months were reported to MORC with tracking identifiers QRA-BKT-2026-002 through -005. Performance remained within pre-established tolerances; two amber signals were recorded in January and April 2026 related to elevated dispersion during earnings weeks. MORC recorded no actions beyond continued monitoring given the transient and contextually explained deviations.

7.3 Operational Monitoring and Alert Handling
QSYS operational monitoring covers data receipt timing, transform completion, model scoring latency, and downstream publish confirmation. Alerts are classified into informational, amber, and red, with route rules to the QSYS Command Center (QCC) staffed by QPE operations analysts, 06:00–22:00 local market coverage with on-call rotation thereafter. Over the review window, 5,412 alerts were logged: 92.6% informational, 6.8% amber, and 0.6% red. No red alerts required MORC escalation. Five amber alerts (INC0019726, INC0019881, INC0020119, INC0020440, INC0020574) were selected for detailed review. Root causes included: delayed corporate action downstream confirmation during peak filings (two cases), stale vendor flags on an alternate FX feed (one case), and recalibration run queueing during a maintenance window (two cases). Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for the sample averaged 14 minutes; mean time to resolve (MTTR) 3.6 hours. All incidents had complete notes, clear ownership transitions, and cross-references to related problems where applicable.

7.4 Incident and Problem Management
Internal Audit examined 30 incident tickets and 8 problem records associated with QSYS during the period. Service availability during defined trading hours was 99.95%, with two partial degradations on 2026-03-11 and 2026-05-02 attributable to extended batch windows intersecting pre-open health checks. Neither event resulted in missed valuation cutoffs or client reporting impacts. Post-incident reviews were completed within five business days in 100% of cases, with captured actions centered on runbook clarification, provider communication enhancements, and scheduling annotations for known cyclical volume spikes. Problem investigations (PRB000317, PRB000322) consolidated recurring low-severity alerts into a single thematic review addressing seasonal corporate action throughput; both remain open with monthly status to MORC and target closure in 2026-07.

7.5 Capacity and Cost Observability
Capacity metrics indicate stable headroom. Average model scoring latency at the 95th percentile was 1.8 seconds for equities and 1.2 seconds for FX workloads, within the defined thresholds. Compute utilization during peak windows averaged 63% across the primary analytics clusters, with episodic spikes to 78% during quarterly rebalances. Storage consumption trends are consistent with onboarding volumes; FY2026 YTD growth for normalized datasets was 7.1%, slightly below the 8–10% projected range due to de-duplication improvements applied in January 2026 (Change CHG0017029).

Cost observability reports (FIN-Ops-QSYS-2026Q2) show a +1.8% variance versus budget for April–May 2026, primarily driven by additional sandbox concurrency authorized for stress testing in preparation for new index methodology scenarios (QPE request QSYS-SBX-Req-2026-04-03). Enterprise Infrastructure confirmed the variance is within tolerance and tied to time-bound analysis commitments, with reversion to baseline forecasted for Q3.

7.6 Compliance and Documentation Hygiene
Documentation hygiene across runbooks, control descriptions, and model documentation showed measurable improvement. Of the 56 artifacts sampled, 55 were current to within 90 days, and one runbook (RB-QSYS-FX-Intraday v3.2) was updated during fieldwork to reflect revised alert taxonomies (commit QPE-Docs-2026-05-21 16:03Z). Evidence retention for change approvals, validation attestations, and PIRs was complete, with traceability across systems using consistent identifiers. Quarterly attestations by control owners (QPE, DGO, MDO) were filed timely and matched operational practices observed.

Overall, the control environment supporting QSYS change management, model governance, and operational monitoring is functioning effectively, with minor timing variances and documentation updates tracked through standard processes. Management has acknowledged the open corrective actions and has provided target dates and accountable owners. No high-severity findings were raised for the period under review.
Section 5: Technology Change, Release, and Configuration Management

5.1 Change and Release Management — Design and Operating Effectiveness

Audit procedures covered the end-to-end governance of application and analytics changes across the Quantitative Systems (QS) estate, including code repositories, orchestration layers, data transformation pipelines, and analytical model packages. The audit evaluated adherence to Meridian Capital’s SDLC Standard SD-14 (rev. 2025.4) and the Enterprise Change Management Policy CMP-001 (rev. 2026.1). The assessment focused on design adequacy of controls, operating effectiveness during FY2026 (Q1–Q3), and alignment with risk appetite statements overseen by the Model Governance Office (MGO). We performed walkthroughs with Quant Platform Engineering (QPE), Production Operations (ProdOps), and the Enterprise Release Management Office (ERMO); inspected artifacts in Jira (Project key: QSYS), ServiceNow Change (CHG), and Confluence; and conducted sample-based testing of 32 production changes (population: 611 changes, 2025-10-01 to 2026-06-30). Sampling targeted standard changes (n=12), normal changes (n=16), and emergency changes (n=4), with coverage across model deployment, batch orchestration, and data schema evolution.

Control design is assessed as sound. The QS Deployment Framework (QSDF v3.6) enforces gate checks comprising peer code review (two-person approval minimum), automated unit and regression test execution, artifact signing, and segregation of duties between developers and release approvers. Promotion paths (DEV → QA → UAT → PRD) are consistently documented in the release record with environment-specific validation steps and rollback criteria. A weekly Change Advisory Board (CAB) convened by ERMO (Tuesdays, 14:00–14:45 ET) documents risk, impact, and scheduling decisions; minutes are cataloged under MC-QS-CAB-2026-xx. The QS-specific release calendar (ref. RELCAL-QS-2026) delineates cut-off windows and blackout periods coordinated with downstream finance close cycles.

Operating effectiveness is rated satisfactory with minor opportunities for standardization. Of the 32 sampled changes, 31 (96.9%) had complete pre-implementation approvals captured in ServiceNow prior to deployment time; one change (CHG-2026-2198, implemented 2026-04-19 22:17 UTC) exhibited an approval timestamp recorded 7 minutes post-deployment due to a documented workflow latency. Subsequent investigation (Problem ticket PRB-2026-0098) confirmed the approval had been granted contemporaneously via CAB consent (minutes MC-QS-CAB-0419) and that the record sync deferred the write-back. All changes evidenced peer review (GitLab MR approvals: dual sign-off), with test pipelines executed successfully (pipeline refs: GL-P-87412 through GL-P-87443). Emergency changes (n=4) followed the designated post-implementation review path within 48 hours, with PIR attachments present (PIR-2026-EM-003, -006, -009, -011) and explicit validation of stability across the following batch cycle.

We observed consistent use of implementation plans and backout descriptions. However, content quality varied in specificity for batch orchestration changes. Three records (CHG-2026-2031, CHG-2026-2147, CHG-2026-2450) referenced generic rollback notes without cross-referencing the precise DAG identifiers and pause criteria documented in the QS Orchestration Catalogue (QORC-Index). While not impeding safe execution, ERMO agreed that a standardized rollback narrative template would enhance clarity and reduce interpretive variability for the overnight ProdOps team. An enhancement request (RFE-2026-0119) was logged on 2026-06-12 to revise the change form and add mandatory fields for orchestration asset IDs and validation probes.

We re-performed linkage testing for traceability from business requirement to deployment artifact for nine sampled changes. Each had a Jira user story or epic with acceptance criteria, evidence of UAT sign-off (RAT and DSO stakeholders), and traceable build hashes in the release ticket. Notably, the model recalibration release QSYS-EPIC-3821 (deployed 2026-05-03 01:12 UTC; CHG-2026-2344) demonstrated exemplary traceability, including attached model validation memos (MGO-VAL-2026-052, 2026-04-26) and a production verification plan with pre/post key performance indicator snapshots.

Forward-fix handling for two minor defects introduced in release wave 2026.06 (INC-2026-07482, INC-2026-07511) adhered to the emergency path with controlled scope and documented risk acceptance by the QS Service Owner (QS-SO-01). No evidence of developer self-approval was observed; approvers were from separate teams and roles per CMP-001. Release deferrals due to fiscal close blackout were appropriately rescheduled with customer communication records present (COMM-2026-CLS-07).

Conclusion: Controls are designed appropriately and operate effectively. We rate this area Low residual risk. Management has initiated process enhancements (RFE-2026-0119) to standardize rollback documentation for orchestration assets. Target completion: 2026-09-30. Responsible: ERMO in partnership with ProdOps and QPE.

5.2 Configuration Management and Baseline Integrity

We assessed configuration governance for QS compute, storage, orchestration, and analytics runtimes to determine whether assets are inventoried, baselined, and monitored for unauthorized drift. The scope included configuration items (CIs) in the Enterprise CMDB tagged with Service: Quantitative Systems (ServiceNow filter: svc=QS, status=Active), associated code-based configuration repositories, and parameter sets referenced by the orchestration layer.

Inventory completeness is materially adequate. As of 2026-06-30, 1,284 CIs are registered under QS, comprising application services (n=214), batch workflows (logical CIs; n=411), data domains (n=93), and platform nodes/containers (n=566). Coverage for production CIs is 98.9% based on reconciliation with QPE’s internal deployment registry (QREG-2026-Q2), with four logical workflows identified as deployed but not yet reflected as discrete CMDB entries (Remediation task CMDB-2026-144). Non-production coverage is 96.2% and improving per the quarterly campaign led by the Data Strategy Office (DSO).

Baseline standards are defined in Configuration Standard CS-07 and QS-Specific Parameter Baseline QPBL-2026. Golden configurations are versioned in Git with change history. We validated baseline alignment for a random sample of 25 production CIs. Twenty-four CIs (96%) matched the approved baseline; one CI (QSB-PRD-ETL01) showed a non-material variance in a scheduling parameter introduced for throughput tuning and subsequently ratified in CAB on 2026-05-10 (CHG-2026-2412). Drift detection is automated via daily comparison jobs with alerts routed to ProdOps (Queue: OPS-QS-CFG). Alert handling metrics for FY2026 YTD show 98.6% of configuration variance alerts triaged within 24 hours (SLO ≥ 95%). We traced six variance tickets (CFG-ALRT-2026-1032, -1041, -1105, -1127, -1183, -1219) and confirmed proper investigation, documentation, and where applicable, update of the gold baseline following approval.

We examined role-based access for configuration updates across code repositories and CMDB. Access reviews were performed on 2026-03-31 and 2026-06-30 (certification campaigns ACCREV-QS-2026-C1 and C2) with no exceptions requiring urgent revocation. The reviewer sign-offs by QS Service Owner and ERMO are documented with timestamps and scope lists. Sensitive parameter sets (e.g., pricing tolerances, retry limits, batch cut-offs) are stored in parameter stores with change history retained; our review confirmed that all parameter changes in scope followed CHG workflow linkage.

Configuration documentation is current and accessible in Confluence (space: QS-CONFIG). Cross-references between CMDB CI records and documentation URLs are present in 92% of sampled items; ERMO has opened a housekeeping task (DOC-LNK-2026-072) to close the linkage gaps. Routine spot checks of orchestration catalog entries (QORC-Index) indicate consistent tagging of owners, support groups, and environment residency.

Conclusion: Configuration management practices are effective, with minor documentation linkage gaps under remediation. Residual risk is Low.



5.3 Incident and Problem Management — Control Assessment

The audit reviewed incident handling across the Quantitative Systems service during FY2026 YTD (2025-10-01 through 2026-06-30), evaluating timeliness, classification accuracy, escalation, communication, and post-incident learning. Data sources included ServiceNow Incident (INC), Problem (PRB), and Change (CHG) modules; PIR repositories; and operations metrics dashboards owned by ProdOps. Interviews were conducted with on-call leads from QPE and the Risk Analytics Team (RAT). Population statistics: 214 incidents logged, categorized as Sev1 (n=2), Sev2 (n=19), Sev3 (n=117), Sev4 (n=76). Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) across all severities: 6m22s; mean time to resolve (MTTR): 1h47m. For Sev1/Sev2, MTTA averaged 2m41s and MTTR 48m.

We examined a stratified sample of 20 incidents, focusing on higher-severity cases and recurring symptom clusters. Representative records included INC-2026-07482 (2026-05-09 03:14 UTC, Sev2, batch orchestration lag), INC-2026-06831 (2026-04-21 21:37 UTC, Sev2, external vendor feed delay), and INC-2026-05219 (2026-03-08 12:05 UTC, Sev1, analytics node resource contention). All sampled incidents had complete initial triage notes within the first 15 minutes, documented communication to stakeholders per the notification matrix (QS-NOTIFY-2026), and assignment to the correct resolver groups. Escalations to MGO for model output variances (n=3) were timely and included interim risk assessment statements.

Root cause categorizations for the full population concentrate in four domains: upstream dependency latency (31%), orchestration dependency configuration defects (18%), data quality rule triggers resulting in protective halts (17%), and environment resource contention (12%). The remaining 22% were single-occurrence operational anomalies (e.g., scheduling deferrals during fiscal close, ad hoc remediation of malformed input files). Problem tickets were raised for all Sev1/Sev2 incidents and for recurring Sev3 incidents once recurrence thresholds were met. Of the sampled incidents, 13 had linked Problem records (PRB-2026-0081, -0094, -0107, -0110, -0113, -0121, -0128, -0132, -0135, -0139, -0142, -0146, -0151), each with a defined hypothesis, corrective actions, and verification-of-effectiveness dates. Problem closure evidencing demonstrated sustained stability across at least two complete batch cycles.

Post-Incident Reviews (PIRs) were completed within the policy timeline (Sev1 within 5 business days, Sev2 within 10 business days). Quality scoring by ERMO (template PIR-QS-2026 v2.1) averaged 3.7/4.0 across the sampled set. We noted strong practice in clearly describing impact windows with precise timestamps and affected business processes. Opportunities were observed in standardizing the recording of “first failure detection point” where monitoring alerted downstream rather than at the initial delay; in three PIRs, the detection narrative could more explicitly differentiate between signal and symptom. An improvement task (OPS-IMP-2026-045) was raised on 2026-06-07 to update PIR guidance text and examples.

Communication to stakeholders met timeliness targets. Incident bridges were opened promptly for Sev1/Sev2 events, and summary updates were disseminated at intervals aligned to severity. Customer satisfaction surveys (CSAT) returned for 38 incidents averaged 4.5/5. We observed consistent closure codes and reason mapping, improving trend analysis fidelity over prior year.

Conclusion: Incident and problem management controls are functioning effectively. Residual risk is Low, contingent on ongoing enhancements to PIR clarity around detection points. Action owner: ProdOps; due date: 2026-09-15.

5.4 Performance and Capacity Management — Monitoring and Forecasting Adequacy

The audit assessed whether QS has appropriate mechanisms to monitor, analyze, and forecast performance and capacity to meet service level objectives. Scope encompassed compute clusters supporting analytics workloads, batch orchestration throughput, and data store performance, as well as forecasting activities overseen by QPE in collaboration with Enterprise Capacity Planning (ECP). Our procedures reviewed quarterly capacity plans (QCP-QS-2026-Q1/Q2), utilization dashboards, and the outcomes of synthetic workload tests conducted pre-close periods.

Overall utilization across the QS compute estate remained within target bands (55–75%) during peak windows. FY2026 YTD peak 95th percentile utilization measured 71%, with headroom estimated at 28% under modeled growth scenarios through FY2027 Q1. Batch orchestration throughput met or exceeded SLOs in 98.7% of cycles; the exceptions correlated with vendor dependency delays, not intrinsic capacity constraints. Queue depth and critical-path latency metrics suggest that recent pipeline optimizations (Release wave 2026.05; CHG-2026-2281, -2287) reduced end-to-end processing time by a median of 8.3% without increased error rates.

Performance regressions, where observed, were contained and addressed via targeted tuning under formal change control. The Problems PRB-2026-0110 and PRB-2026-0132 addressed environment contention and non-optimal parallelism parameters, respectively. Verification-of-effectiveness tests following parameter adjustments reported stable performance across ten consecutive business days, with no adverse side effects. The ECP quarterly forecast, updated 2026-06-21, incorporates business growth inputs from the Front Office Technology Roadmap (FOTR-2026-H2) and projects a 14–18% increase in compute demand; planned capacity augmentation has been sequenced to avoid fiscal close windows and includes scenario buffers.

Monitoring coverage is robust. Key indicators (throughput, latency at defined checkpoints, job retries, and resource saturation warning signals) are visualized in role-based dashboards. Alert thresholds are calibrated against historical baselines and SLOs. In the sampled set of performance alerts (ALRT-PERF-2026-2017, -2031, -2042, -2059), triage notes show timely review and either dismissal (false positive) or escalation to change requests where warranted. Documentation supporting the monitoring inventory and alert tuning is maintained and current.

We noted two process improvement areas. First, while capacity plans are timely and conservative, the explicit linkage between business initiatives and their quantified footprint could be made more transparent for non-technical stakeholders; ECP has agreed to augment narratives in QCP-QS-2026-Q3 with business-aligned impact statements. Second, a minority of performance dashboards use legacy naming conventions for pipeline stages; QPE has scheduled a unification task (QPE-STD-2026-033) to align nomenclature with the QORC-Index, improving cross-team comprehension.

Conclusion: Performance and capacity management effectively support service objectives. The control environment is mature with minor enhancements underway to improve stakeholder communication and dashboard standardization. Residual risk is Low.

Section 5.2 Data Ingestion and Quality Controls: Test Results

Internal Audit completed fieldwork over the period 2026-05-02 to 2026-06-14 covering data ingestion, validation, and reconciliation controls within Quantitative Systems (QSYS). Evidence was obtained from operational logs, the enterprise data catalog, and control attestations maintained by the Data Governance Office (DGO) and Quantitative Engineering (QE). The scope targeted market data, reference data, and derived analytics inputs for production models hosted in environment ID ENV-PROD-QSYS-01. Tested controls mapped to control library items QSYS-DQ-01 through QSYS-DQ-07 and DG-LIN-02. The review period for metric sampling was FY2026 Q2 (2026-02-01 to 2026-04-30), unless otherwise noted.

Ingestion timeliness controls were evaluated against documented service-level objectives (SLOs) of 99.5% on-time delivery for daily vendor feeds and 99.0% for intraday tick aggregates. Across 5.2 million records and 183 daily schedule instances, on-time performance averaged 99.2% for daily feeds and 99.3% for intraday aggregates. The audit assessed data quality and lineage controls across Meridian Capital’s Quantitative Systems (QSYS) for FY2026 (period: 01 Jul 2025 through 30 Jun 2026), focusing on front-to-risk market data pipelines, pricing reference datasets, risk factor timeseries, and trade/position enrichment flows stewarded by Risk Data Services (RDS) and the Quantitative Engineering (QE) organization. Methodology
Procedures included: (a) sampling 28 business-critical data elements across seven pipelines (sample count: n=420 data records per element spanning five business days per quarter), (b) review of lineage capture in the Enterprise Data Governance Catalog (DGC) for selected elements, (c) reconciliation of control totals between source and consumer systems, (d) evaluation of data quality rule execution records in the RDS rules engine (Rule IDs DV-119, DV-204, DV-311, DV-404), and (e) inspection of incident and defect tickets relating to data quality (ServiceNow INC and JIRA QSYS series) for root cause and remediation follow-through. Evidence was time-bounded to FY2026 and anchored to control attestations TRC-CTRL-DA-12.3 and TRC-CTRL-DG-04.2, with witness testing by Technology Risk & Controls (TRC) completed on 2026-06-12 15:20 UTC.

Results and Observations
- Completeness: Across sampled pipelines, average daily completeness for mandatory fields was 98.7% (min 97.9%, max 99.4%) against a documented threshold of ≥98.5%. Minor shortfalls were observed in RDS-MDS-PRD-311 on 2026-02-14 due to late-arriving vendor files; ServiceNow ticket INC0109234 (opened 2026-02-14 13:45 UTC; resolved 2026-02-14 15:02 UTC) indicates on-time backfill with no downstream breach of RAE calculation windows.

Section 9. Data Quality and Reconciliation Controls (Field Testing Results and Follow-Up)

Scope and approach
Internal Audit reviewed the design and operating effectiveness of data quality and reconciliation controls across the Quantitative Systems data supply chain supporting market risk, liquidity risk, and front-office analytics for the period 2026-04-01 through 2026-06-30. The review encompassed inbound vendor market data (equity, rates, FX), internal reference data masters, trade/position extracts from core books-and-records platforms, and downstream computed measures (end-of-day P&L, sensitivities) within the QS-Risk platform. Primary systems in scope included QS-ETL-17/19 (ingestion and transformation), QS-DQ-Rules (data quality rules engine), QS-LIN-02 (lineage registry), and QS-RISK-AGG (risk aggregation services). Control families assessed were: DQ-01 field-level validation, DQ-02 completeness and timeliness checks, DQ-03 reconciliation to authoritative sources, DQ-04 exception governance and escalation, and DQ-05 lineage and metadata maintenance. Samples were risk-based and judgmental, totaling 30 operating days for high-volume feeds (MD_EOD_EQ, FX_SPOT_L1) and 12 operating days for lower-volume reference datasets (ISSUER_LEI_MAP, HOLIDAY_CAL).

Operating effectiveness testing
Testing confirmed that routine field-level validations (type, null, cardinality, referential integrity) executed as configured and produced exception files with appropriate tagging for downstream triage. For example, on 2026-05-03T05:42:11Z, ETL job QS-ETL-17 initiated ingestion for MD_EOD_EQ and completed at 2026-05-03T05:58:42Z, processing 2,345,221 equity quotes; QS-DQ-Rules flagged 1,411 records (0.06%) with null securityId, all auto-quarantined and excluded from publication per SOP-DQ-014. The Market Data Operations (MDO) queue SNOW INC00274932 recorded investigation start at 2026-05-03T06:12:03Z and closure at 2026-05-03T10:27:54Z following vendor confirmation of a partial upstream index constituent update. Audit verified timely closure and attachment of vendor case transcript (Ref: VND-CASE-584113).

Timeliness checks under DQ-02 were evaluated against service windows documented in OLA-MDO-QS-2026. For FX_SPOT_L1, the defined T+0 publication SLA is 06:00:00Z with a 10-minute grace threshold. Over the 30-day sample, 29 days met SLA; on 2026-06-12 publication completed at 06:14:09Z (breach of grace threshold). Ticket SNOW PRB0009123 captured root cause as a transient delay in vendor circuit switchover during scheduled maintenance; MDO correctly invoked the exception protocol and notified downstream stakeholders via the QS status channel at 06:17:41Z (Ref: STA-ALRT-2026-06-12-01). No downstream calculation runs were materially impacted; QS-RiskCalc runs were deferred by 15 minutes in accordance with the runbook, and Trading Analytics acknowledged deferral at 06:19:05Z (Teams thread link retained in the problem record).

Reconciliation outcomes
Reconciliation controls (DQ-03) between QS-computed end-of-day P&L and the Finance authoritative ledger (GL_RPT_EOD) were reviewed for a stratified sample of five trading books across Rates and FX. Differences were within established tolerances (≤ 5 bps of notional) for 17 of 20 sampled book-days. Three instances exhibited immaterial but above-nominal variances (max 7 bps, dated 2026-05-10, 2026-05-17, 2026-06-07 for book IDs RATES_LDN_02 and FX_NY_03). Root cause analysis documented in JIRA QS-3129 attributed the variance to a rounding configuration mismatch introduced by the QS-RISK-AGG v3.2.1 upgrade, wherein the summation of leg-level P&L applied bank rounding in one component and round-half-up in another. The Quantitative Systems Engineering (QSE) team aligned parameters in CHG0071289 (deployed 2026-06-11T22:08:34Z), and subsequent reconciliations on 2026-06-12 and 2026-06-13 fell within baseline tolerances. Audit validated evidence of management review and sign-off by Finance Controls (email approval 2026-06-12T12:43:09Z, Ref: FIN-CTRL-APPR-6821).

Lineage and metadata maintenance
Data lineage artifacts in QS-LIN-02 were found to be substantially current. Sampled lineage chains for MD_EOD_EQ → QS-ETL-17 → QS-DQ-Rules → QS-RISK-AGG are traceable with dataset versioning and transformation notes present. Two lineage nodes required update: the addition of the volatility surface interpolation step introduced in QS-RiskCalc build 2026.05.14.3 was not reflected in the lineage register for dataset RISK_SENS_GAMMA_V1 and the deprecation of intermediate staging table STG_EQ_754 was not marked as retired. JIRA QS-3274 was raised by Data Engineering to update the lineage registry; closure recorded on 2026-06-21T09:04:26Z with peer review by Enterprise Data Governance Office (EDGO).

Reference data quality
The ISSUER_LEI_MAP dataset exhibited a 0.4% rate of unmapped legal entity identifiers during the April sample week, driven by recent corporate actions. Exceptions were appropriately triaged with EDGO via ticket EDG-REF-2026-0412, and backfills were processed by 2026-04-15. Controls verifying golden source alignment with the Legal Master were performed as per SOP-REF-005, and an enhancement request (QS-ENH-1987) was logged to extend the one-to-many mapping logic to accommodate cross-listed entities, with target delivery in the FY2026 Q4 roadmap.

Archival and retention checks
Retention adherence for market data snapshots was examined for MD_EOD_EQ and FX_SPOT_L1 in the archival store QS-ARC-01. For January 2026, two days (2026-01-08 and 2026-01-21) displayed partial snapshot archival (94% and 96% completion respectively) due to nightly storage tiering lag. The Data Platform team remediated through a re-index operation executed under CHG0069742 on 2026-03-04T01:22:51Z. Evidence of complete backfill and verification scans is attached to SNOW TASK RCT0005419. No retention period breaches were observed; WORM settings confirmed as configured for seven-year retention on relevant buckets. Audit notes that monitoring dashboards were updated to include a “percent of partition archived” metric (Grafana panel QS-ARC-P07) as of 2026-05-02.

Exception governance and reporting
Exception volumes and handling were consistent with thresholds documented in DQ-KPIs-2026. Monthly average exception rate across all in-scope datasets was 0.11%, with 98.7% of exceptions closed within the two-business-day target. KPI breach observed on 2026-05-06 for FX_SPOT_L1 due to vendor remediation delay; waiver approved by Data Governance Council (DGC) in meeting minutes DGC-2026-05-09. Audit verified that waivers were time-bound and did not alter underlying control expectations.

Conclusion and recommendations
Overall, the control environment for data quality and reconciliation within Quantitative Systems is operating effectively, with exceptions detected, triaged, and resolved in accordance with established procedures. Minor enhancements are recommended: (1) formalize a playbook step for validating deterministic rounding settings post-release to risk aggregation services (action logged under QS-ENH-2041, owner: QSE), and (2) include lineage update checkpoints in the release checklist to ensure QS-LIN-02 updates occur concurrently with deployments (change template update requested in CAB-NTC-2026-06-18). Management agreed with recommendations and provided target completion dates between 2026-08-15 and 2026-09-30. No high-severity findings were raised in this area.



Section 10. Change and Release Management Review (QS Platforms)

Scope and methodology
Internal Audit assessed the design and effectiveness of change and release management controls applied to Quantitative Systems platforms for the period 2026-04-01 to 2026-06-30. The review focused on the QS-RISK application stack (calculation engines and aggregation services), QS-ETL ingestion pipelines, and the QS-DQ-Rules engine. The evaluation covered a population of 18 production changes categorized under ITSM taxonomy as normal (13), standard (4), and emergency (1). Evidence sources included ServiceNow change records (e.g., CHG0071289, CHG0071330, CHG0071412), CAB minutes, Git repository commits (QS-Risk repo, refs 5b1f9c2 and d7e34a1), CI/CD pipeline logs (Build 2026.05.14.3; Artifact ID QS-Risk-3.2.1-20260514), UAT sign-offs, and post-implementation review (PIR) documents. Interviews were conducted with Quantitative Systems Engineering (QSE), Risk Technology Quality Engineering (RTQE), IT Service Management (ITSM), and Trading Analytics stakeholders between 2026-06-18 and 2026-06-25.

Planning and approvals
For the sample of 12 normal changes tested in detail, all change records included documented scope, risk impact assessments, test evidence, and backout strategies consistent with SOP-CHG-101. Approval workflows were appropriately executed with recorded endorsements from the Application Owner (QSE Director), RTQE Lead, and Business Owner (Head of Trading Analytics) prior to implementation. For example, CHG0071289 (QS-RISK-AGG parameter alignment) received approvals at 2026-06-10T16:22:11Z (RTQE), 2026-06-10T17:05:29Z (Business Owner), and 2026-06-10T18:14:03Z (App Owner), aligning with the documented deployment window of 2026-06-11T22:00:00Z–23:00:00Z. CAB minutes CAB-2026-06-09 reflect discussion of dependencies and confirmation of non-overlapping changes in adjacent systems.

Segregation of duties and traceability
A SoD test across a stratified sample of 10 changes confirmed that no developer merged or deployed their own code to production. Git merge requests associated with CHG0071330 (DQ rules threshold refinement), MR-2145 and MR-2147, demonstrate peer review by separate QSE engineers and approvals by RTQE prior to pipeline promotion. CI/CD artifacts retained immutable build hashes (e.g., SHA-256: 3c1a8f...e7b4) and mapped unequivocally to change IDs within the deployment log QS-DEP-LOG-2026Q2. Audit observed consistent bi-directional linkage: each change record linked to its MR and pipeline execution; each pipeline run included the originating change ticket number and CAB approval reference.

Testing and quality gates
RTQE executed unit, integration, and regression test suites as per TEST-RTQE-PLAN-2026Q2. For the QS-RiskCalc 3.2.1 release (Build 2026.05.14.3), unit test coverage was reported at 84% (threshold ≥ 80%), with 1,204/1,204 unit tests and 312/312 integration tests passing. Performance benchmarks indicated stable run times (median 27m14s vs baseline 27m09s). UAT sign-off for functional changes was captured via Trading Analytics approvals (emails at 2026-05-16T13:41:22Z and 2026-05-30T09:02:47Z). One normal change (CHG0071412, ETL loader optimization) failed initial UAT due to a non-functional defect in a monitoring counter; the change was rescheduled and released after defect remediation (JIRA QS-3291; re-approval at 2026-06-22T15:28:56Z). No production incidents were attributable to changes released in the period; incident trend analysis (ITSM-MET-INC-2026Q2) corroborated zero change-related service degradations.

Emergency and standard changes
The single emergency change (CHG0071359, applied 2026-05-24T04:18:03Z) addressed a configuration misalignment detected in a non-critical downstream batch schedule, preventing a potential delay in a weekend reporting cycle. Evidence shows adherence to the emergency protocol with expedited approvals from the Duty Manager and App Owner, documented PIR within 48 hours (PIR-2026-05-26), and no downstream impact. Standard changes (four occurrences) followed pre-approved templates with automated deployment steps and did not require CAB review; audit confirmed that the standard change catalogue (CAT-STD-CHG-2026) is current and that each standard change instance referenced the correct template version.

Release calendar discipline and communications
Deployments occurred within designated maintenance windows (Thursdays 22:00–23:59Z and Saturdays 02:00–04:00Z) with one exception: CHG0071412 was rescheduled to Saturday 04:15Z–05:00Z following UAT re-run, with CAB endorsement for the adjusted window. Stakeholder notifications were issued with ≥ 48 hours advance notice for normal changes and ≥ 24 hours for standard changes, per COMM-CHG-STD. Sampling of four change notifications confirmed distribution lists included Trading Desks, Market Risk, MDO, and Operations Control, and that notifications contained concise business impact statements and validation steps for post-deployment checks.

Post-implementation review and monitoring
PIRs were present for all normal and emergency changes sampled and included validation of success criteria, observation windows (typically T+1 business day), and metrics review. Post-change monitoring showed stable key technical indicators: ETL job runtimes within ±3% of baseline, QS-RISK-AGG memory utilization unchanged, and DQ exception rates not elevated post-release. For CHG0071330 (DQ rules refinement), Audit verified that the intended reduction of false-positive alerts for stale FX ticks materialized (from 0.09% to 0.05% of records) without suppressing legitimate alerts; RTQE provided a two-week comparative analysis (ANL-RTQE-2026-06-15).

Documentation and minor observations
Change templates and runbooks were complete and aligned to SOP-CHG-101, with backout steps specific and tested in pre-production environments. Audit noted two minor documentation gaps: (1) CHG0071289 lacked an explicit dataset dependency enumeration for a downstream ad hoc sensitivity report (resolved prior to deployment via addendum at 2026-06-11T15:03:41Z); and (2) decommissioning of a feature toggle introduced for testing (FT_QS_GAMMA_OPT) did not have a closure checklist entry in the change record, though the toggle was removed in code and validated by RTQE. QSE agreed to update the change template to include a “dataset/report dependency” field and a “feature toggle disposition” checkbox (action item CAB-ACT-2026-06-23-02; due 2026-08-01).

Conclusion and recommendations
Change and release management controls for Quantitative Systems are designed and operating effectively. Evidence supports disciplined planning, approvals, testing, and post-implementation monitoring, with strong segregation of duties and traceable lineage from change request through deployment. Internal Audit recommends: (1) embedding explicit dataset/report dependency mapping into all normal change records; (2) expanding the PIR template to prompt verification of feature toggle removal where applicable; and (3) continuing quarterly drills of backout procedures for high-impact components to maintain operational readiness. Management accepted recommendations with target completion dates spanning 2026-08-01 to 2026-09-15. No medium or high-severity findings were raised in this domain for FY2026 Q2.
Section 7. Change Management and Release Governance (continued)

7.2 Release Pipeline Controls and Audit Testing
Internal Audit evaluated the design and operating effectiveness of release governance for Quantitative Systems between 2025-10-01 and 2026-03-31. The review encompassed 31 production releases, inclusive of three expedited maintenance releases, executed by Quant Engineering (QE) in coordination with Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) and the Enterprise Change Control Board (ECCB). Evidence was sourced from ServiceNow change records (CRQ-2026-0154, CRQ-2026-0229, CRQ-2026-0311, et al.), Helix build artifacts (Build IDs HELIX-ML-2026.0213.1042 through HELIX-ML-2026.0330.1915), and ECCB minutes (ECCB-Min-2026-Q2-04 dated 2026-03-28 15:00 UTC). Across the sample, all releases demonstrated documented business rationale linked to approved work items (e.g., QSYS-4217, QSYS-4450, DEF-2026-019), traceability to source commits, and a standardized deployment checklist referencing pre-implementation validation and post-implementation verification (PIV).

Automated gate controls embedded in the release pipelines required successful execution of unit/regression test suites, static model conformance checks, and artifact immutability confirmation prior to promotion from staging to production. Internal Audit confirmed, via sampled log reviews (pipeline runs 2026-02-14 09:27 UTC; 2026-03-12 20:43 UTC), that these gates fired consistently and blocked deployment pending attestation from QE release managers and SRE approvers. For all 31 releases, evidence showed the ECCB recorded dual approvals with separation of duties upheld, notably with requesters and approvers belonging to distinct reporting lines (QE vs. SRE vs. MRM), in accordance with Meridian Capital Standard CHG-PROC-2026 v3.2.

The review also assessed rollback preparedness and recovery posture. Each sampled release contained a documented and tested rollback plan with version references and operational steps aligned to Release SOP REL-SOP-QSYS-05 Rev 4.1. PIV tasks, recorded under ServiceNow task IDs (e.g., TASK-2026-11874; TASK-2026-12402), confirmed normal system operation and key dataset availability within the prescribed window. Median time to complete PIV was 34 minutes (range 18–42 minutes) for standard releases and 51 minutes for maintenance releases, driven by extended validation of model output aggregates following data refresh windows. No deviations from the required one-hour PIV completion target were observed.

7.3 Ticketing, Approvals, and Evidence Completeness
A reconciliation was performed between ServiceNow change tickets, JIRA work items, and repository tags to test end-to-end traceability. Internal Audit matched 100% of selected changes to an originating JIRA ticket (e.g., QSYS-4398 for parameter harmonization in the calibration service; QSYS-4511 for dependency uplift in the analytics container) and verified that commit hashes captured in the change form aligned with the repository tag at deployment (Helix tag QNTS-PLD_v2026.03.12.1 mapped to commit a1f3c7d on 2026-03-12 20:11 UTC). ECCB meeting notes recorded approvals with timestamps that predated the production deployment window by a minimum of two hours, satisfying lead time requirements for stakeholder review.

Evidence completeness was assessed against the documentation checklist in CHG-CHECK-2026 Annex B. Across the sample, attachments included deployment plans, back-out plans, pre-deployment sign-off, and validation screenshots from the monitoring console (Report IDs MON-REP-2026-02-14-0912 and MON-REP-2026-03-12-2049). Three records (CRQ-2026-0197, CRQ-2026-0243, CRQ-2026-0276) contained attachments where the file naming convention did not align with the standard prefix (expected “REL-YYYYMMDD-<system>-<env>”); however, the content was complete and clear, and the variance did not impede review. QE rectified the naming on 2026-03-29 10:07 UTC after notification (ServiceNow task TASK-2026-13011), and SRE updated the pre-deployment checklist to include a quick visual confirmation of filenames during ECCB prep. No instances were identified where control execution depended on the attachment naming scheme; thus, the observation is considered low significance.

7.4 Maintenance Releases and Expedited Path Controls
Three maintenance releases (CRQ-2026-0205, CRQ-2026-0239, CRQ-2026-0291) utilized the expedited path defined under CHG-FAST-2026 v2.0, limited to non-functional updates such as configuration consistency and library minor-version alignment. Internal Audit verified that the expedited criteria were met, that scope limitation attestations were completed by QE leads, and that MRM was informed via distribution list MRM-Notify@ 24 hours prior to change. Post-deployment telemetry indicated stable service performance with no capacity or latency impacts. Each expedited change included a completed risk/impact assessment referencing business continuity classifications and documented fallback to the prior container image, satisfying policy conditions without exception.

7.5 Findings and Conclusion on Change Governance
Based on the procedures performed, control design and operating effectiveness for change governance within Quantitative Systems are rated Effective. All changes were authorized, tested, and implemented in accordance with policy; separation of duties was maintained; and PIV activities confirmed service stability. Minor housekeeping improvements were identified regarding attachment naming consistency and have been addressed. No material issues, no control breakdowns, and no unapproved changes were observed during the review period. Management’s response, recorded under MGMT-RESP-2026-QSYS-07 dated 2026-04-05 13:22 UTC, concurs with the results and confirms continued monitoring by QE and SRE in quarterly control self-assessments (CSA IDs CSA-QSYS-2026-Q2 through CSA-QSYS-2026-Q4).



Section 8. Model Performance Monitoring and Data Lineage Oversight

8.1 Monitoring Framework and MRM Oversight
Internal Audit reviewed the model monitoring framework applied to key Quantitative Systems models, including RS-CRD-Alpha (credit risk classification), RS-MKT-Beta (market microstructure signal), and FX-LIQ-Gamma (liquidity forecast), as cataloged under MRM register entries MRM-REG-ALPHA-012, MRM-REG-BETA-019, and MRM-REG-GAMMA-007. The framework is governed by MRM-POL-2026-01 and MRM-STND-VAL-2026-02, with operational processes described in QE-MON-SOP-08 Rev 3.2. Evidence from the enterprise monitoring console (Dashboards QMET-ALPHA, QMET-BETA, QMET-GAMMA), monthly MRM attestations (MRM-ATTEST-2026-02 and MRM-ATTEST-2026-03), and alert tickets (ALR-2026-0449, ALR-2026-0511) indicated that monitoring controls operated consistently throughout the period.

Thresholds for classification performance, calibration stability, and drift statistics are documented at the model level and reviewed quarterly by MRM. For RS-CRD-Alpha, area under the ROC curve (AUC) remained within the 0.82–0.85 band, with February and March point estimates of 0.836 and 0.842, respectively. Expected calibration error (ECE) tracked at 1.7%–2.1%, comfortably within the 3.0% internal alert threshold. RS-MKT-Beta exhibited a realized signal-to-noise ratio consistent with the backtesting corridor (+/- 8% relative to baseline), while FX-LIQ-Gamma’s RMSE declined 2.3% quarter-on-quarter following the January feature preprocessing refinement (QSYS-4387), as evidenced by HELIX-ML-VAL report VAL-2026-01-27-1530.

Alert handling procedures demonstrated timely triage and closure. Two transient alerts (ALR-2026-0449 on 2026-02-11 07:16 UTC; ALR-2026-0511 on 2026-03-07 21:39 UTC) were triggered by upstream data latency within the permissible recovery window. Finance Data Operations (FDO) acknowledged and resolved the condition within 43 and 58 minutes, respectively, with no breach of model output delivery SLOs. MRM reviewed and documented the non-materiality of the events (MRM-REVIEW-2026-0449, MRM-REVIEW-2026-0511) and confirmed no re-calibration was indicated.

8.2 Data Quality Controls and Lineage Verification
Audit procedures assessed the completeness and accuracy of data quality (DQ) rules applied to the model feature stores and the end-to-end lineage documentation for core datasets. The Data Governance Office (DGO) maintains authoritative lineage records in the enterprise catalog for Data Assets DA-QSYS-CRD-01 (credit bureau aggregates), DA-QSYS-MKT-02 (market microstructure features), and DA-QSYS-FX-03 (FX liquidity metrics). The lineage diagrams (DCAT-QL-1982, DCAT-QL-2055, DCAT-QL-2110) traced source systems to curated feature stores (FS-ALPHA-01, FS-BETA-02, FS-GAMMA-01) and onward to model scoring services (SRV-ALPHA-SCR, SRV-BETA-SIG, SRV-GAMMA-FRC). Internal Audit verified that lineage metadata reflected current ETL flows (ETL-JOB-DFX-17, ETL-JOB-DFX-22, ETL-JOB-DFX-31) and that business and technical stewards were correctly assigned.

DQ rules, as registered in DGO-DQ-SET-ALPHA v2.4 and DGO-DQ-SET-GAMMA v1.9, included checks for schema conformity, mandatory field completeness, range validation for key indicators, and referential integrity for joins across primary keys. Sampled execution logs (DQ-RUN-2026-02-13 05:02 UTC; DQ-RUN-2026-03-15 05:04 UTC) showed pass rates of 99.6% and 99.7%, respectively, with the small fraction of warnings attributable to known late-arriving data from a non-critical enrichment feed. These warnings auto-resolved within the designed reconciliation window and were documented in FDO tickets DQ-2026-118, DQ-2026-131. No critical or high-severity DQ exceptions were recorded during the period.

Lineage freshness controls require quarterly certification by data stewards. For DA-QSYS-FX-03, the certification (CERT-2026-Q1-FX dated 2026-03-22 14:11 UTC) confirmed an unchanged flow and re-validated transformation descriptions. Internal Audit noted one instance where the lineage diagram for DA-QSYS-MKT-02 displayed a “stale” indicator for 48 hours following a minor nomenclature update to a staging table (STG_MKT_TICKS_V12 to STG_MKT_TICKS_V12A). The indicator cleared automatically after the next scheduled metadata harvest (2026-03-26 02:00 UTC), and DGO documented the event in CAT-OPS-2026-077 without customer impact or downstream ambiguity. The observation is classified as low significance; lineage accuracy remained intact throughout.

8.3 Metrics Summary, Service Levels, and Observations
Service level adherence for model monitoring and data operations remained strong. Model scoring timeliness for RS-CRD-Alpha met the 99.5% on-time threshold, recording 99.7% over the review period. FX-LIQ-Gamma batch completion met its 95th percentile completion target of 35 minutes, with an observed 95th percentile of 32 minutes and a maximum of 44 minutes during an extended market data load on 2026-03-08. Data completeness for critical fields across the three feature stores averaged 99.9%, with null rates for monitored features not exceeding 0.3% in any run reviewed. Population Stability Index (PSI) for monitored features remained below 0.08 across monthly comparisons, indicating stable input distributions without evidence of material drift.

Governance artifacts were current and accessible. Model fact sheets (MFS-ALPHA-v2026.03; MFS-BETA-v2026.02; MFS-GAMMA-v2026.03) included clearly enumerated monitoring thresholds, responsible owners, and escalation paths. Quarterly MRM sign-offs (MRM-SO-2026-Q1 dated 2026-03-29 16:45 UTC) confirmed that monitoring outputs were reviewed, that alerts were appropriately triaged, and that any trend deviations were explained and documented. The Quant Engineering team maintained a log of monitoring queries and enhancements under QSYS-ENH-4602 and QSYS-ENH-4621 focused on visualization clarity and aggregation windows; both items remain scheduled for completion in FY2026 Q3 per the product roadmap.

Conclusion for Section 8
The monitoring and data lineage environment for Quantitative Systems is operating effectively. Controls are well-defined, metrics are stable, and governance documentation is current. Internal Audit identified only low-significance, self-resolving observations (temporary lineage staleness indicators), with no adverse impact on model performance, reporting, or consumer understanding. No remediation actions are required. Management has acknowledged the observations in MGMT-RESP-2026-QSYS-08 (2026-04-05 13:26 UTC) and will incorporate minor usability improvements in the upcoming monitoring dashboard refresh cycle.
Section 4.3 — Change Management Review (Quantitative Systems)

The Internal Audit team assessed the end-to-end change management lifecycle for Quantitative Systems (QSys) across model code, analytics libraries, and supporting orchestration components used by Risk Analytics and Investment Platforms during FY2026 Q2–Q4. The review encompassed standard releases, hotfixes, and maintenance updates flowing through the enterprise change tooling stack (Jira, ServiceNow, Git-based version control, and Jenkins/Airflow CICD orchestrators). Evidence was collected under Evidence Pack EP-QSYS-FY26-4.3, with sampling stratified by risk classification and deployment environment (DEV, UAT, PROD). The sample included 36 production-bound changes (QSYS Jira tickets QSYS-2188, QSYS-2261, QSYS-2314, QSYS-2339, QSYS-2372, QSYS-2391, QSYS-2417, QSYS-2440, QSYS-2476, QSYS-2501, and 26 additional items), mapped to corresponding ServiceNow change records (e.g., CHG-2026-011821, CHG-2026-012045, CHG-2026-012482) with deployment timestamps between 2026-01-12T09:14:07Z and 2026-06-28T22:47:33Z.

Change governance requirements are defined in the QSys Operating Procedures QSYS-OP-02 (rev. 5.1, effective 2026-02-01) and aligned to Corporate IT Change Standard ITC-Std-04. The audit focused on: (i) traceability from business request to code commit and compiled artifact; (ii) documented approvals, including Model Risk Management (MRM) sign-off where applicable; (iii) pre-deployment testing evidence, inclusive of backtesting snapshots for model-affecting releases; (iv) environment promotion controls and deployment windows; and (v) post-deployment validation and ticket closure hygiene. Responsibility for day-to-day execution resides with the Quantitative Engineering team (QEng) and QSys Release Management, with oversight by the Change Advisory Board (CAB-RiskTech), which meets biweekly; attendance records for 2026-03-05, 2026-03-19, 2026-04-02, 2026-04-16, 2026-04-30, and subsequent sessions were confirmed via minutes filed under CAB-RISKTECH-2026-MeetingNotes.

Control design was assessed as appropriate for the complexity and risk profile of the Quantitative Systems landscape. All sampled releases evidenced separation of duties between code authorship and final approver, documented via distinct user identifiers in Jira and ServiceNow. The audit verified that deployment pipelines required a tagged release candidate originating from protected branches in the enterprise Git repository, with peer review indicated by recorded approvals (e.g., QSYS-2417 approved by user ID u107392 at 2026-05-02T13:18:22Z). For model-impacting changes, MRM concurrence was visible in attachment MRM-NC-2026-141 (QSYS-2391) and MRM-NC-2026-155 (QSYS-2476), each with pre- and post-change performance deltas documented. Jenkins promotion logs were matched to ServiceNow implementation windows to validate execution within authorized timeframes; no deviations were detected.

Release cadence and outcomes over the review period demonstrate consistent throughput with controlled risk. The function executed 11 standard releases in Q2, 13 in Q3, and 12 in Q4, with two hotfixes in May and one in June categorized as “Expedited—Low Risk,” each pre-approved by CAB-RiskTech Chair under CHG-2026-012612, CHG-2026-012781, and CHG-2026-012943. Of the 36 sampled releases, 34 progressed with no production incident linkage within seven days post-deployment. Two releases (QSYS-2339, deployed 2026-04-11T21:06:51Z; QSYS-2501, deployed 2026-06-22T00:14:39Z) triggered non-material defects in downstream batch orchestration (Airflow DAG latency warnings) that were remediated within 8 hours via configuration adjustments documented in Jenkins job logs and Airflow run IDs AF-2026-04-12-883 and AF-2026-06-22-091. No rollbacks were executed, and no trading or client reporting SLAs were breached.

Testing artifacts were comprehensive and reproducible. Unit test coverage for core analytics libraries (qsys-core, qsys-stats) averaged 84.7% across the sampled period, as evidenced in Jenkins coverage reports JRPT-2026-05-02 and JRPT-2026-06-18. Integration test results including synthetic portfolio evaluations were attached in the Jira tickets for model-impacting changes; for example, QSYS-2476 included backtest result CSVs and a summary memo dated 2026-06-12T10:41:03Z authored by the Quantitative Validation team, indicating stable performance metrics within predefined tolerances. UAT sign-off by Risk Analytics Product Owners was present for 100% of sampled releases labeled “User-Visible,” with e-signatures captured in ServiceNow tasks TS-2026-44831, TS-2026-45207, and others.

Change documentation hygiene met expected standards with minor opportunities to strengthen timeliness. Specifically, 3 of the 36 sampled change records (CHG-2026-012045, CHG-2026-012482, CHG-2026-012781) were administratively closed 1–2 business days after the defined post-implementation review window, despite the PIR notes being available on time in the ticket activity logs. Audit interviews with QSys Release Management on 2026-06-29 confirmed the delay was due to batching of closure tasks during a resource transition and did not affect operational oversight. Additionally, tag descriptions in the Git repository for 4 releases did not include a link-back to the ServiceNow change ID; however, the linkage was clear in Jira and Jenkins, and traceability from requirement to deployment remained intact.

Based on the evidence, the operating effectiveness of change controls for Quantitative Systems during the period reviewed is rated Satisfactory. The process is consistently executed, approvals are complete and timely, and risk-based gates (including MRM concurrence where required) are adhered to. The noted documentation timing and metadata link-back observations are characterized as low-severity administrative items. Management acknowledged the observations during the closing meeting on 2026-07-02 and indicated that a lightweight enhancement to the release checklist (QSYS-CHK-Rel-2026 rev. 1.3) to prompt Git tag annotation will be included in the July sprint, with internal tracking under Jira process task QSYS-PROC-118.
